meta.title: French — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 43 spellings, silent letters, accents and liaison — start here, beside DELF A1
meta.desc: How French is read, before or beside the first word: 43 notes, one card each — 16 vowel spellings (a, e, ai, au and eau, eu, i, o, oi, ou, u, y and the nasal vowels an, en, in, on, un and oin), 17 consonant spellings and word endings whose sound is not the English one (c, ch, g and gu, gn, h, j, -ill-, ph, qu, r, s between vowels, th, ti before a vowel, x, the final consonants that are not said, -er and -ent), and 10 rules: the five accents (é, è, ê, ë, ç), the ligature œ, elision (l', j', d'), liaison (les‿amis), the mute and the aspirated h, and the space French puts before ? and !. The front shows the letters. The back gives, for each position the letters can stand in, the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the example words of the article it is taken from, then up to three words of the DELF A1 deck with a speaker beside each, the letters picked out, and the pronunciation that word's own card prints. Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. Of DELF A1's 476 cards, 103 are single words ending in a d, p, s, t, x or z that is not said, and 68 of its 484 headword forms carry an accent. THE ORDER is the vowels, the nasal vowels, the consonants in alphabetical order, the word endings, then the rules. At Folio's default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 5 days; it is meant to be studied beside DELF A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: no description is written for this deck and no English comparison is offered, the source giving none. Each position, sound and set of examples is a row of the spelling-to-sound tables of the article named below, usually its major value, with a minor value or an exception quoted beneath where a beginner meets it; each rule is a passage of the article named on its line, with a cut marked […]. A row is carded only where a one-word DELF A1 headword shows it, in spelling and in the pronunciation its card prints, so the letters that sound as an English speaker expects (b, d, f, k, l, m, n, p, t, v, z) have no card. French stress has none either: the articles do not treat it. The speaker is your device's French voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — Spellings and sounds, the accents, œ and the punctuation: Wikipedia, “French orthography”, revision 1385602140 of 2026-11-14. Liaison: “Liaison (French)”, revision 1383148088 of 2026-11-01. Elision: “Elision (French)”, revision 1334000091 of 2026-01-21. The aspirated h: “Aspirated h”, revision 1348655490 of 2026-04-13 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, pronunciations and meanings: the DELF A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0; sentences from Tatoeba, CC BY 2.0 FR).

fields.Name: the acute accent — accent aigu
fields.Says: An acute accent over ⟨e⟩ represents /e/. An ⟨é⟩ in modern French is often used where a combination of ⟨e⟩ and a consonant, usually ⟨s⟩, would have been used formerly, e.g. écouter ← escouter.
fields.Examples:
as in
l'été/e.te/ · summer
l'école/e.kɔl/ · school
le café/ka.fe/ · coffee

fields.Name: the grave accent — accent grave
fields.Says: A grave accent over ⟨a⟩ or ⟨u⟩ is primarily used to distinguish homophones: à ("to") vs. a ("has"); ou ("or") vs. où ("where"; ⟨ù⟩ is used only in this single word). A grave accent over ⟨e⟩ indicates /ɛ/ in positions where a plain ⟨e⟩ would be pronounced /ə/ (schwa).
fields.Examples:
as in
à/a/ · to
où/u/ · where
le père/pɛʁ/ · father

fields.Name: the circumflex — accent circonflexe
fields.Says: A circumflex over ⟨a, e, o⟩ indicates /ɑ, ɛ, o/, respectively, but the distinction between ⟨a⟩ /a/ vs. ⟨â⟩ /ɑ/ is being lost in Parisian French, merging them as [a]. […] A circumflex over ⟨i, u⟩ does not change their sound […]. Most often, it indicates the historical deletion of an adjacent letter (usually ⟨s⟩ or a vowel): château ← castel, fête ← feste, sûr ← seur, dîner ← disner
fields.Examples:
as in
être/ɛtʁ/ · to be
la fenêtre[fə.nɛ.tʁə] · window
l'hôtel/o.tɛl/ · mansion

fields.Name: the diaeresis — tréma
fields.Says: A diaeresis over ⟨e, i, u, y⟩ indicates a hiatus between the accented vowel and the vowel preceding it, e.g. naïve /naiv/, Noël /nɔɛl/.
fields.Examples:
as in
Le 24 décembre est la veille de Noël.December 24th is Christmas Eve.

fields.Name: the cedilla — cédille
fields.Says: A cedilla under ⟨c⟩ indicates that it is pronounced /s/ rather than /k/. […] The cedilla is only used before ⟨a, o, u⟩, e.g. ça /sa/. A cedilla is not used before ⟨e, i, y⟩, since they already mark the ⟨c⟩ as /s/, e.g. ce, ci, cycle.
fields.Examples:
as in
ça/sa/ · that
le garçon/ɡaʁ.sɔ̃/ · boy
français/fʁɑ̃.sɛ/ · French

fields.Name: e dans l'o
fields.Says: ⟨œ⟩ […] is a mandatory contraction of ⟨oe⟩ in certain words. Some of these are native French words, with the pronunciation /œ/ or /ø/, e.g. chœur "choir" /kœʁ/, cœur "heart" /kœʁ/, […] sœur "sister" /sœʁ/, œuf "egg" /œf/ […]. It usually appears in the combination ⟨œu⟩; œil /œj/ "eye" is an exception.
fields.Examples:
as in
l'œuf/œf/ · egg
la sœur/sœʁ/ · sister

fields.Name: elision — élision
fields.Says: In French, elision (élision) is the suppression of a final unstressed vowel (usually /ə/) immediately before another word beginning with a vowel or a silent ⟨h⟩. The term also refers to the orthographic convention by which the deletion of a vowel is reflected in writing, and indicated with an apostrophe.

fields.Name: liaison
fields.Says: In French, liaison is the pronunciation of a linking consonant between two words in an appropriate phonetic and syntactic context. For example, the word les ('the') is pronounced /le/, the word amis ('friends') is pronounced /ami/, but the combination les amis is pronounced /lez‿ami/, with a linking /z/. Liaison only happens when the following word starts with a vowel or semivowel, and is restricted to word sequences whose components are linked in sense, e.g., article + noun, adjective + noun, personal pronoun + verb, and so forth.

fields.Name: the mute h and the aspirated h
fields.Says: In French spelling, aspirated "h" (h aspiré) is an initial silent letter that represents a hiatus at a word boundary, between the word's first vowel and the preceding word's last vowel. At the same time, the aspirated h stops the normal processes of contraction and liaison from occurring. […] Since the phonological behavior of aspirate h words cannot be predicted through spelling, usage requires a considerable amount of memorisation.

fields.Name: the space before a mark
fields.Says: In France, Belgium, and Switzerland, the exclamation mark, question mark, semicolon, colon, percentage mark, currency symbols, hash, and guillemet all require a narrow no-break space between the punctuation mark and the material it adjoins. […] This rule does not apply in Canadian French, where a space is inserted only before colons, brackets, and dashes and between guillemets and the quoted text.
fields.Examples:
as in
Est-ce que tu comprends ?Do you understand?
Entrez, s'il vous plaît !Please come in!
Excusez-moi !Excuse me!
